246.

Book Eight, of the
Kings and Lords, and of
the manner that they had
in their elections,
and in the governance
of their
Kingdoms.
✠

Prologue.

According to what the old men affirm, in whose keeping were the paintings and
memories of ancient things: those who first came to settle
this land, this New Spain, came from the north, in
search of the earthly paradise. They bore as their name Tamoanchan,
which is what is now called "tictemoa tochan," meaning "we seek our
natural home." Perhaps induced by some oracle that one of
the most esteemed among them had received and spread abroad: that the earthly
paradise lay toward the south, as is true, according to almost all
who write, that it lies beneath the equinoctial line. And they settled
near the highest mountains they could find, having heard
that there is an exceedingly high mountain, which is indeed true. These first settlers, as
the most ancient buildings, now very evident, show,
were: an exceedingly robust people, most wise, and most warlike. Among
other very notable things that they did, they built a city, most fortified,
in a most opulent land, of whose happiness and riches, even in
its ruined buildings, there are great signs. This city they
called Tullan, which means "place of fertility and abundance," and it is
still called so today, and it is a very pleasant and fertile place. In this city
there reigned for many years a king called Quetzalcoatl, a great sorcerer
and inventor of sorcery, which he left to his descendants, and to this day they
practice it. He was extraordinary in moral virtues. The affair of this King
holds among these natives the same place as that of King Arthur among the English. This
city was destroyed, and this King driven out; they say he traveled toward
the east, that he went to the city of the sun, called Tlapallan, and was
called "of the sun." They say he is alive, and that he must return to reign
and rebuild that city which was destroyed; and so to this day they await
him. And when Don Hernando Cortés came, they thought he was him, and
as such they received and kept him, until his conversation, and that of
those who came with him, undeceived them. Those who fled from this city
built another very prosperous city, called Cholula, which,
for its nobility, buildings, and grandeur, the Spaniards, upon seeing it,

they gave it the name Rome. It seems that the affair of these two cities
followed the path of Troy and Rome. After this, for many years
the Mexican nation began to grow populous, and in about three hundred years,
more or less, they came to rule over the greater part of the kingdoms and
lordships that exist in all that is now called New Spain; and they
founded the city of Mexico, which is another Venice. Its lords
were emperors, especially the last one, who was Motecuçoma: a man
very brave, very warlike, and skilled in arms; magnanimous,
and of great ability, and magnificent, exceptional in matters of
justice, though cruel. In his time the Spaniards arrived, and there had
already been many prophecies that they were to come in his time. Once
the Spaniards arrived, the empire of the Mexicans ended, and the destruction
began. And because there are many notable things in the manner of governing
that these infidels practiced, this volume was compiled, which deals with the lords
and with all their customs.

251

Book Eight

The elder Motecuhzoma, the first Motecuhzoma, was the fifth lord of Tenochtitlan: he ruled over the people of Mexico for thirty years. He also waged wars against the province of Chalco, and against those of Cuauhnahuac, and against all the subjects of the aforementioned capital, and against those of Macahuacan. In his time there was a very great famine, lasting four years, which was called "the eating of rabbits" (necetochviloc); because of this, the people of Mexico, and those of Tepaneca, and those of Acolhuacan scattered to other places to seek their livelihood.

Axayacatl was the sixth lord of Mexico, and he ruled for fourteen years. In his time there was war between the people of Tenochtitlan and those of Tlatelolco. The people of Tlatelolco lost their lordship because of the victory that the people of Tenochtitlan won over them; and for this reason, the people of Tlatelolco had no lord for a period of forty-six years. The one who was then lord of Tlatelolco was called Moquihuix. The said Axayacatl conquered and won these towns or provinces: Tlacotepec, Cozcacuauhtenanco, Calimaya, Metepec, Calixtlahuaca, Tecaltepec, Teutenanco, Malinaltenango, Tzinacantepec, Coatepec, Cuitlapilco, Teotzitlahuacan, Tequaloya, and Ocuilan.

...milca

The fifth ruler of Tenochtitlan.

The elder Motecuhzoma was the fifth ruler of Tenochtitlan. He ruled for thirty years, and he made war and brought rain upon all the Chalca and the people of Cuauhnahuac, and upon all who called themselves people of Cuauhnahuac, and upon Macahuacan. In his time there occurred a great famine; it lasted four years, and it was called "the eating of rabbits," during which all the Mexica, the Tepaneca, and the Acolhuaque scattered.

The sixth ruler of Tenochtitlan.

Axayacatl was the sixth ruler of Tenochtitlan. He ruled for fourteen years. During his reign, the Tlatelolca and the Tenochca made war upon each other; when they fought, the rulership of Tlatelolco was destroyed, and for forty-six years no one ruled as lord of Tlatelolco. When this war took place, the one who ruled in Tlatelolco was named Moquihuix. And this Axayacatl conquered Tlacotepec, and Calimaya, and Metepec, Calixtlahuaca, Tecaltepec, Cozcacuauhtenanco, Teutenango, Malinaltenango...

of the kings, and lords of Mexico.
fo. 2.

Ticocicatzin was the seventh lord
of Tenochtitlan, and he held that office for four years,
and in his time there was no war.

Ahuitzotl was the eighth lord of
Tenochtitlan, for a period of eighteen
years, and in his time the city
of Mexico was flooded, because he ordered
that five springs be opened, which
are located on the boundaries of the towns
of Coyoacan and of Huitzilopochco. And
the springs have these names:
Acuecuexatl, Tlilatl, Huitzilatl, Xo
chcaatl, Coatl: and this happened four
years before the death of the said
Ahuitzotl, and twenty-two years
before the coming of the Spaniards.
Also in his time there occurred a very
great eclipse of the sun, at midday,
lasting about five hours, and there was
a very great darkness, so that the
stars appeared: and the people felt
very great fear, and they said that
monsters called tzitzimime were going
to descend from the sky and devour
men and women. The said Ahuitzotl
conquered these provinces: Tziuhcoac,
Molanco, Tlapan, Chiapan,
Xaltepec, Izoatlan, Xochtla,

Tzinacantepec, Coatepec, Cuitlapilco, Teo
xahualco, Tequaloya, Ocuillan.

¶ Here is the seventh ruler
of Tenochtitlan.

Ticocicatzin ruled as the seventh ruler in
Tenochtitlan for four years. Nothing
notable happened during his reign.

¶ Here is the eighth ruler
of Tenochtitlan.

Ahuitzotl ruled as the eighth ruler in
Tenochtitlan for eighteen years and three
[more]. At that time Mexico was flooded,
by his order it was done, so that five
caves were opened, whose names are:
Acuecuexatl, Tlillatl, Huitzillatl, Xoch
caatl, Coahuatl; the waters rose and
flooded Huitzilopochco: it continued rising
for four more years, until Mexico was
flooded, before Ahuitzotl died. And when
the Spaniards came, it had been twenty-two
years since Mexico had been flooded:
and at that time there also occurred an
eclipse of the sun, at midday: it darkened
for about five hours, the stars appeared,
and there was great fear; it was said
that the tzitzimime would descend
and devour people: and he [Ahuitzotl]
conquered Tziuhcoac, and Molanco,
Tlapan, Chia...

252

Book Eight.

...amaxtlan, mapachtepec, xoconochco, Aiutlan, maçatlan, coiacan.

[illustration of a seated lord]

The ninth king of Mexico was Motecuçoma, the second of this name: and he reigned nineteen years, and in his time there was a very great famine, for a period of three years, (it was unrelenting); because of this the people of Mexico scattered to other lands. In his time there also occurred a marvel in Mexico: in a great house, where people gathered to sing and dance, a great beam that lay across the walls sang like a person—this was the song: "Veya noqueztepole, vel xomjotia, atlantiuetztoce," which means: "Woe to my shoulder, dance well, for you will be lying in the water." This happened when the fame of the Spaniards was already spreading through this land of Mexico. Also in the time of this same Motecuçoma, the demon called Cioacoatl went about at night weeping through the streets of Mexico, and everyone heard her saying: "O my children, woe is me, for I must leave you." Another sign occurred in the time of Motecuçoma: a woman, a neighbor of Mexico Tenochtitlan, died of an illness, and was buried in the patio, and on top of her grave they placed some stones...

[continuing the place names from the previous page]: ...pan, xaltepec, içoatlan, xochtlan, amaxtlan, mapachtepec, xoconochco, aiutlan, maçatlan, coiocan.

¶ The ninth, ruler of Tenochtitlan.

Motecuçuma, the ninth, ruled in Tenochtitlan for nineteen years. In his time there was a famine of two years in which it did not rain, and so the Mexica people suffered greatly, afflicted everywhere by the famine. Also in his time, it happened that a wooden beam that was in a house in Tenochtitlan sang in the middle of the night, lamenting, saying: "Veiah noqueztepole uel xomjotia, atlatiuetztoce" ("Woe, my shoulder, dance well, for you lie fallen in the water"). This happened just before news came of the Spaniards. Likewise, it happened that the woman-serpent (Cioacoatl) went about weeping at night; everyone heard her weeping, saying, "My beloved children, now I must truly leave you." This also happened. died of sickness; then
she was placed in the courtyard. After

Of the Kings [lords] of Mexico, Book Eight

...auhco, iolloxonecuillan, atepec,
Mictlan, Hoapan, nopallan, iztec
Tlalocan, cuextlan, quetzaltepec,
Chichioaltatacalan.

[ornamental woodcut border]

In his time also, eight years before the coming of the Spaniards, there appeared and frightened the people something that rose up at night, a sort of glow of brightness, like a flame of fire, and it lasted all night, and it was born from the direction of the east, and it disappeared when the sun was about to rise; and this was seen for four years in a row, always at night: and it disappeared four years before the coming of the Spaniards. And in the time of this lord, the Spaniards came to these lands, who conquered the city of Mexico, where they presently reside, and all of New Spain: which conquest took place in the year one thousand five hundred and nineteen.

The tenth lord who ruled Mexico was called Cuitlahua, and he held the lordship [the text continues onto the next column]...

[Nahuatl text, parallel to the Spanish, naming the same places: Çocollan, Tecoma Ixtlauaca, Çacatepec, Tlachquiauhco, Iolloxonecuillan, Atepec, Mictlan, Hoapan, Nopalan, Iztectlalocan, Cuextlan, Quetzaltepec, Chichioaltatacalan.

It also happened in his time that, eight years before the Spaniards arrived, something was seen — people were terrified; at night it rose up, very bright, like a fire burning, lighting the night as if it were daybreak, and when the sun was about to rise it vanished. This occurred every night for four years, and then it ceased. Four years later the Spaniards arrived, and it was in that same time that the Spaniards came and conquered Mexico, where they now reside everywhere in New Spain, in the year one thousand five hundred and nineteen.]

Here is the tenth ruler of Tenochtitlan.

Cuitlahua, the tenth ruler...

de los reyes, y señores de Mexico [Of the kings and lords of Mexico]                                    folio 4

...eighty days [had passed] since the Spaniards were already in Mexico, and during this time a great mortality, or pestilence of smallpox, occurred throughout the land. This illness had never before happened in Mexico, nor in any other land of this New Spain, according to what the elders used to say. It disfigured everyone's faces, for it caused many pockmarks upon them, and so many were those who died of that illness that there was no one left to bury them. For this reason, in Mexico they threw the dead into the canals, since at that time there was a very great abundance of water; and a very great stench arose from the dead bodies.

The eleventh lord of Tenochtitlan was called Quauhtemoc, and he governed the people of Mexico for four years. In his time the Spaniards conquered the city of Mexico and all the surrounding region. Also in his time there arrived and came to Mexico the twelve friars of the order of Saint Francis, who have converted the natives to the holy Catholic faith, and...

[Nahuatl column, parallel account:]
In Mexico Tenochtitlan: it was eighty days since the Spaniards had arrived in Mexico. At that time there occurred a great sickness, a great pestilence, by which people died everywhere in every town; it was called "the great rash," "the great pustules." For the first time it was seen — nowhere in Mexico had it been seen before — it caused people's faces to break out; it became rough and pitted. No longer could the dead be carried out [for burial]; they simply threw them into the water, for at that time there was a great deal of water everywhere in Mexico, and it was very deep; thus the dead were cast away.

¶ The twelfth ruler of Tenochtitlan.

Quauhtemoc ruled as the twelfth lord of Tenochtitlan; he reigned for four years. During this time the Spaniards conquered and took the city of Mexico, and in this way the conquest spread everywhere, over every town. At that time twelve friars arrived [in New Spain]...

254

Book Eight

They and the other ministers have destroyed the idols, and planted the Catholic faith, in this New Spain.

The twelfth governor of Tenochtitlan was called don Andrés Motelchiuh, and he governed three years, in the time of the Spaniards: with whom he took part in the conquests of the provinces of Cuextlan, and of Honduras, and Anáhuac. Afterwards he went with Nuño de Guzmán to conquer the lands of Culhoacan, and there he ended his life.

The thirteenth governor of Tenochtitlan was called don Pablo Xochiquen, and he governed the people of Mexico for three years.

The fourteenth governor of Tenochtitlan was named Don Diego Huanitl, and he was governor for four years.

The fifteenth governor of Tenuch[titlan]...

[of the fathers of] Mexico

The priests, children of Saint Francis, went to abolish idolatry, and they taught the Christian faith.

Twelfth ruler of Tenochtitlan.

Don Andrés Motelchiuh, the twelfth, ruled in Tenochtitlan: in the year of the Spaniards, he went everywhere to conquer Cuextlan and Honduras, and with Nuño de Guzmán he went to conquer great Culhoacan, where he died.

Thirteenth ruler of Tenochtitlan.

Don Pablo Xochiquen, the thirteenth, ruled in Tenochtitlan for three years.

Fourteenth ruler of Tenochtitlan.

Don Diego Huanitl, the fourteenth, ruled in Tenochtitlan for four years.

Fifteenth ruler of Tenochtitlan.

Don Diego Tehuetzquiti, the fifteenth...

Of the kings and lords of Tlatelulco. fol. 5.

...titlan, he was named don Diego Tehuelquiti, and he governed for thirteen years: and during his time there occurred the great mortality and pestilence in New Spain: and it came out like water from the mouths of the men and women, naturally, a great quantity of blood: on account of which infinite people were dying and did die: and because in each house there was no one to take charge of the sick, many died of hunger: and every day in every town many dead were buried. And also in the time of the said don Diego there was the war with the Chichimecs of Suchipila, which don Antonio de Mendoza waged, he who was the first viceroy of New Spain.

The sixteenth governor of Mexico was called don Cristóbal Cecepatic, and he governed four years.

¶ Chapter Two, of the lords who reigned in Tlatelulco before they lost the lordship: and afterward, when it was restored to them by the Spaniards, until the year 1560.

The first lord of Tlatelulco was called Quaquapitzahuac, and he governed the people of Tlatelulco for sixty-two years: and he conquered the people of Tenayuca, and those of Coatlalco, and those of Xaltocan: and he governed while being lords of Tenochtitlan...

[Nahuatl text:] ...he ruled in Tenochtitlan: thirteen years passed, and during this time a great sickness occurred, called pestilence, which came from the nose; blood flowed greatly, by which many died; and also many died of hunger, continuously for twenty years; and during that time many perished — the Chichimeca were conquered, as were the Xochipiltecah and the people of Sacapolal.

¶ The eighteenth ruler of Tenochtitlan.

Don Cristóbal Cecepatic, the eighteenth, ruled in Tenochtitlan for four years.

¶ Here begins the second chapter, which tells of the rulers who ruled in Tlatelulco, before the rulership was lost, and afterward, when the Spaniards gave it back again and restored it to them, up until the year 1560.

¶ The first ruler of Tlatelulco, Quaquapitzahuac, first began to rule in Tlatelulco for sixty-two years; he conquered the people of Tena[yuca]...

Book eight

...titlan, the ones already mentioned, in the first
chapter, Acamapichtli, and Huitzilihuitl.

The second lord of Tlatelolco,
was called Tlacateotl, and he governed
the people of Tlatelolco for thirty-eight
years: and in his time the lands of Acolhuacan
and of Coyoacan were conquered.

The third lord of Tlatelolco, was
called Cuauhtlatoa, and he governed for
thirty-eight years: and he governed in the time
of two lords of Tenochtitlan,
named above, Itzcoatl, and
Huehue Motecuhzoma: and in his time
the provinces of
Azcapotzalco, and of Coaixtlahuaca,
and of Cuetlaxtlan, and of Cuauhtinchan,
and of Xochimilco, and of Cuauhnahuac
were conquered.

The fourth lord of Tlatelolco, was called...

...and the people, and Coatlan, and
Xaltocan, Michoacan, and they were ruled
and met together with both
lords in Tenochtitlan who were
named: Acamapichtli and
Huitzilihuitl.

¶ Here is the second ruler of Tlatelolco.

Tlacateotl was the second to rule
in Tlatelolco, for twenty
years and eighteen more, during which
all of the Acolhuacans and the Coyoacans
were conquered.

¶ Here is the third ruler of Tlatelolco.

Cuauhtlatoa was the third to rule in
Tlatelolco, for twenty years and
eighteen more years, and he ruled together
with the two lords who ruled
in Tenochtitlan, namely Itzcoatl and
Huehue Motecuhzoma. During this time
the Azcapotzalcans were destroyed and
conquered, and the Coaixtlahuacans, and
the Cuetlaxtecans, and the people of Cuauhtinchan,
and the people of Xochimilco, and all
the people of Cuauhnahuac.

¶ Here is the fourth ruler of Tlatelolco.

...mo Moquiuixtli, who governed for nine years; and during his time the lordship of Tlatelolco was lost, because of the hatred and enmity that existed between him and his brother-in-law, the lord of Tenochtitlan, called Axayaca; and in the end, being defeated and desperate, the said Moquiuixtli climbed the steps of the temple of his idols, which was very tall, and from the top of the said temple he threw himself down, and so his life ended.

Don Pedro Temilo, afterward, in the time of the Spaniards and after the conquest of Mexico, was governor of those of Tlatelolco, and thus the people of Tlatelolco came to recover their lordship; and this Don Pedro took part with the Spaniards in the conquests of the provinces of Cuextlan, and of Honduras, and of Guatemala.

Don Martín Ecatl was the second governor of those of Tlatelolco after the conquest of those of Mexico, and he governed for three years; and during his time the devil, who went about in the form of a woman appearing by day and by night and was called Cihuacoatl, ate a child that was in its cradle in the town of Azcapotzalco. Also during his time it happened...

Moquiuixtli was the fourth to rule as lord in Tlatelolco: for nine years he held the rulership there, until he and his brother-in-law Axayaca, ruler of Tenochtitlan, became enemies, and Axayaca made war upon Moquiuixtli and the people of Tlatelolco. And as for Moquiuixtli himself, he went alone to the top of the great temple, and from there he threw himself down, and there he died.

¶ Don Pedro Temilo, when he was made ruler in Tlatelolco, was the one who once again began the rulership there, after the Spaniards had already conquered the altepetl of Mexico. He went everywhere accompanying the Spaniards when they went to conquer Cuextlan, Honduras, and Guatemala.

¶ Don Martín was the second to rule as lord in Tlatelolco: for three years, during the time of the Spaniards. In his time it happened that a female demon devoured a small child that lay in Azcapotzalco; and also in his time it happened that eagle warriors gathered together in the eagle house, and there was disturbance and unrest there...

Chapter Three, of the
lords of Tezcuco.

The first lord of Tezcuco was called
Tlalteatzin, and he ruled over those of
Tezcuco for only eighty days: and in his
time nothing worthy of memory
was done: and he is called lord
of the Chichimecs.

Book Eight.                                    Of the Prognostics

A little after midnight, [the comet appeared] and lasted until morning, when the sunlight hid it. So that when the sun rose, it no longer appeared; according to some it was seen for a whole year, and according to others, for four years in succession. Whenever this comet appeared at night, all the Indians raised great cries, and were terrified, expecting that some great evil was about to come.

Another evil omen occurred here in Mexico: the temple (cu) of Huitzilopochtli caught fire, with no human cause whatsoever; it seemed that it caught fire miraculously, and flames came bursting out from inside the wooden beams, outward, and it quickly burned down. The priests cried out for water to be brought to put it out, but the more water they threw on it, the more fiercely it burned, until it was entirely consumed.

[Nahuatl text, parallel account:]
The sky stood still, or rather the heavens seemed to turn; thus it was seen to stand there: toward that direction it would rise, just as it went forth at midnight, it was seen to shine forth giving light, and at dawn it would appear. [The star called] Quetzalcoatl would overcome and destroy the sun; at times it would rise and appear; a full year it would reappear (in the year Ten House it began), and when it appeared, it was greatly feared — people would strike their mouths in fear, and give warning cries, and watchers would keep vigil.

As for the second omen that occurred here in Mexico: of its own accord, without being lit, fire suddenly blazed up and burned, no one knowing how it had caught fire, in the house of the god called Huitzilopochtli, named Tlacateccan. From within it the flames leapt forth, tongues of fire, blazing fiercely, and in an instant it consumed everything, all the wooden framework. Then the elders cried out, saying: "O Mexicans, let everyone come running, let it be put out!" with pitchers of water; but however much they tried to extinguish it, the more it blazed, and it could not be put out until it had burned everything away.

The third evil omen that occurred was that a bolt of lightning fell, almost without cause and without thunder, upon the temple of the god of fire called Xiuhtecutli: this temple had a thatched roof of straw, and the lightning fell upon it and set it ablaze, and it burned down. They took this for a miracle, because there had been no thunder, though it was raining lightly.

The fourth omen was that by day, while the sun was shining very clear, a comet came from the west over Mexico and ran toward the east, casting off from itself what looked like embers or great sparks, and it had a very long tail. And then all the people began to cry out together, for it seemed a fearful thing, and for this reason they took it as an omen.

The fifth was that the lake of Mexico, without any wind blowing at all, rose up: it seemed to boil, and the water leapt up high, and it caused a great storm on the lake, and the waves beat against the houses that stood near it, and knocked down many of them. They took this as an omen, because no wind was blowing.

The sixth omen was that in those days they heard voices in the air—
